questions.q: The 1st tower has {m} blocks, the 2nd tower has {m2} blocks and the 3rd tower has {m3} blocks. How many blocks will tower number {n} have?
questions.e: Each tower has {m} more blocks, so tower {n} has {m} × {n} = {ans} blocks.

questions.q: In a plant nursery the rows have {m}, {m2}, {m3}, … plants. If the pattern continues, how many plants are there in row {n}?
questions.e: Row n has {m} × n plants: {m} × {n} = {ans}.

questions.q: A gardener puts 2 pots in the 1st row, 4 in the 2nd, 6 in the 3rd, and so on. How many pots are in row {n}?
questions.e: The rule is ‘add 2’ (even numbers): row {n} has 2 × {n} = {ans} pots.

questions.q: What sequence do we get when we add up odd numbers (1, 1+3, 1+3+5, …)?
questions.e: 1, 4, 9, 16, … – adding the first n odd numbers gives n × n.

questions.q: What is the sum of the first {n} odd numbers?
questions.e: 1 + 3 + 5 + … (first {n} odd numbers) = {n} × {n} = {ans}.

questions.q: The sequence 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, … is called the…
questions.e: Each number is the sum of the two before it: 8 + 13 = 21.

questions.q: The branch of Mathematics that studies patterns in whole numbers is called…
questions.e: Number theory is the study of patterns and relationships among whole numbers.

questions.q: How are the terms of 3, 6, 12, 24, … generated?
questions.a: By multiplying the previous term by 2

questions.q: A regular polygon is a shape with…
questions.a: all sides equal and all angles equal
w: all sides equal but angles different
questions.e: Equilateral triangle, square and regular hexagon are regular polygons.

questions.q: The sequence 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, … is an example of…

questions.q: Is 64 a square number or a cube number?

Assertion (A): The sequence 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, … is an odd number sequence.
Reason (R): The sequence 2, 4, 6, 8, … is an even number sequence.
questions.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
w: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.e: Both statements are true, but the even sequence does not explain why the first one is odd.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): All square numbers can be arranged in equal rows and columns.
Reason (R): Square numbers are formed by multiplying a number by itself.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
w: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.e: n × n means n rows of n – which is exactly a square arrangement.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): All odd numbers are prime numbers.
Reason (R): Odd numbers are not divisible by 2.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
w: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
questions.e: 9, 15 and 21 are odd but not prime, so A is false; R is true.

questions.q: Annual Day LED lights grow in a square pattern: 1, 4, 9, 16 lights. How many lights are needed for Pattern {n}?
questions.e: Pattern {n} is a {n} × {n} square: {ans} lights.

questions.q: A toy shop packs 1, 8, 27 and 64 balls in the first four boxes. How many balls will box number {n} hold?
questions.e: These are cube numbers: {n} × {n} × {n} = {ans}.

questions.q: Square numbers can be shown as dots arranged in…
questions.a: a square with equal rows and columns
questions.e: 16 = 4 rows of 4 dots.

activity.title: Square, cube or both?
activity.say: From your school worksheet: sort each number. Squares are n × n, cubes are n × n × n.
items: Not n × n or n × n × n
